reference.title: arrive in or arrive at?
reference.text: We use arrive in + cities or countries (arrive in Paris, arrive in Brazil) and arrive at + buildings, stations, etc. (arrive at the hotel, arrive at the station). arrive home – no preposition.

reference.title: Prepositions in questions
reference.text: In questions the preposition usually goes at the end: What are you thinking about? Who does this bag belong to? Who are you waiting for?

reference.why: wait always needs for before the person or thing.

reference.wrong: We arrived to London at six.
reference.right: We arrived in London at six.
reference.why: never arrive to: arrive in a city / country, arrive at a building.

reference.title: Connected speech
reference.text: When a word which ends in a consonant sound is followed by one which begins with a vowel sound, the words are linked, i.e. pronounced as one word, e.g. Let’s talk_about your problem. This can make it difficult to understand the individual words.

reference.title: Linked or not linked?
reference.text: think_of, listen_to? No: listen ends in /n/, but to begins with a consonant – not linked. depends_on, arrived_in, worried_about, spend_on – linked (consonant + vowel). wait for, pay for – not linked (for begins with a consonant).

reference.title: An informal email
reference.text: Start: Hi / Dear + name. Thanks for your email. End: Looking forward to hearing from you (= I hope you write again soon). Best wishes / Love + your name. PS = I forgot to say this before. Use contractions (I’m, it’s, we’re).

tasks.instruction: Do the quiz: How organized are you?
tasks.note: SB 1a–d + Communication p.103 (подсчёт баллов): тест без верных ответов → Talk: ИИ задаёт 5 вопросов теста с вариантами, считает баллы по таблице книги и читает результат, потом обсуждение (1d)

exercises.situation: You are a classmate in an English class (level: pre-intermediate). You are doing the quiz ‘How organized are you?’ with the student. Read each question with its three options and ask the student to choose one (they can answer with the letter or in their own words; ask why sometimes). 1 When you have lots of things to do,… a you write them on a piece of paper or a Post-it note. b you keep them in your head. c you put them in your phone, diary, or calendar. 2 When you go shopping,… a you sometimes have a list. b you always have a list. c you decide what to buy when you get there. 3 When you meet friends,… a your friends sometimes arrive before you. b you are usually the first to arrive at the restaurant. c your friends always need to wait for you. 4 When you go on holiday,… a you pack a few hours before leaving. If you’ve forgotten something, you can buy it when you get there. b you have a list of what to take and start packing a few days before. c you look through your wardrobe and pack the night before you go. 5 When you travel by plane or train,… a you arrive at the airport or station a long time before you really need to be there. b you usually arrive at the recommended time. c you leave home at the last possible minute. Scoring: Q1 a=2 b=1 c=3; Q2 a=2 b=3 c=1; Q3 a=2 b=3 c=1; Q4 a=1 b=3 c=2; Q5 a=3 b=2 c=1. After question 5, tell the student their total and read the result: 12–15 You are extremely organized. Are you maybe too organized? How good are you at adapting when your plans change? Try to be tolerant with other people who are not as organized as you are. 9–11 You are organized in some aspects of life, but less in others. Maybe you need to make some small changes. Look at your answers again. Did you score 1 for any of the questions? Are you happy with those answers? 5–8 You are extremely disorganized. Do you know what day it is? Do you know what year it is? Sometimes it’s good to be spontaneous, but you definitely need to be more organized! Then ask: Do you agree with the result? Do you know anybody who is very organized or very disorganized? Tell them your own result too (you scored 10). Keep your language simple.
exercises.goal: Do the quiz and talk about how organized you are.
exercises.opener: Let’s do the quiz! Question 1: When you have lots of things to do, do you a) write them on a piece of paper or a Post-it note, b) keep them in your head, or c) put them in your phone, diary, or calendar?
criteria: answers all five quiz questions
explains at least two answers in full sentences
says if they agree with the result and why
describes a very organized or very disorganized person they know

steps.example: c – I put everything in my phone.

steps.text: Say if you agree with your result
steps.example: I agree. I’m quite organized, but I’m always late.

steps.text: Talk about an organized or disorganized person
steps.example: My brother is very disorganized. He never knows where his keys are.

reference.title: Present continuous for the future
rows: I’m seeing an old friend tonight. She’s arriving at lunchtime.
She isn’t leaving until Friday. They aren’t coming to the party tomorrow.
What are you doing this evening? Is he meeting us at the restaurant?

reference.title: Future arrangements
reference.text: We often use the present continuous for future arrangements, when we have decided the time and place (it’s in our diary): I’m having dinner with Mark Taylor on Tuesday. We usually say when: tonight, tomorrow, on Saturday, next week.

reference.title: be going to or present continuous?
reference.text: We can often use either: I’m going to see Anna on Tuesday. = I’m seeing Anna on Tuesday. The present continuous is very common with tonight, tomorrow, this weekend and with travel verbs go, come, leave, arrive: I’m leaving on Monday is more common than I’m going to leave on Monday.

reference.wrong: I see an old friend tonight.
reference.right: I’m seeing an old friend tonight.
reference.why: Don’t use the present simple for future arrangements.

reference.wrong: Look at the clouds! It’s raining this afternoon.
reference.right: Look at the clouds! It’s going to rain this afternoon.
reference.why: Predictions: be going to, not the present continuous.
